faq.a: Yes; low‑titer TSI may cause subclinical disease or isolated ophthalmopathy.
faq.q: Can TSI be present without hyperthyroidism?

faq.a: Combine with clinical signs and hormone levels; treatment is indicated when thyrotoxicosis is documented.
faq.q: Is a positive TSI test enough to start treatment?

faq.a: Rely on clinical picture, suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, and diffuse goitre; consider trial of antithyroid drug.
faq.q: What if the TSI assay is unavailable?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with weight loss, tremor and a diffuse goitre. TSH is 0.1 µIU/mL, free T4 is high. Which investigation confirms the autoimmune basis and why? — TSI functional assay; a positive result confirms Graves disease and predicts relapse risk.

During a ward round you see a patient with Graves ophthalmopathy but normal thyroid function tests. What explains this and how would you manage? — TSI can stimulate orbital fibroblasts independent of hormone levels; treat eye disease with steroids or orbital radiotherapy, monitor thyroid function.

A patient in a rural hospital has thyrotoxicosis signs but no radioiodine uptake scanner. How do you differentiate Graves from toxic multinodular goitre? — Look for diffuse goitre, presence of exophthalmos, and low TSH; if TSI unavailable, a uniform gland on palpation favors Graves.

You suspect thyroid storm in a patient with fever, tachycardia and altered mental status. What is the immediate priority and does TSI status alter it? — Stabilise airway, give beta‑blocker, iodine, steroids; TSI result is irrelevant in the acute setting.

Why are thionamides preferred as first‑line therapy in most low‑resource settings for Graves disease? — They are inexpensive, orally administered, and effective at blocking hormone synthesis; alternatives like radioiodine need equipment, surgery needs expertise.

A pregnant woman is diagnosed with Graves disease. Which drug class is safest and why? — Propylthiouracil in the first trimester (less teratogenic than methimazole) then switch to methimazole later; avoid radioactive iodine.
Explain how TSI contributes to the development of pretibial myxedema. — TSI cross‑reacts with fibroblast TSHR, increasing glycosaminoglycan deposition in skin, causing non‑pitting edema.
What laboratory pattern would you expect in a patient with subclinical Graves disease? — Normal free T4/T3, suppressed TSH, and positive low‑titer TSI.
ai.title: Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: TSI are auto‑antibodies that bind and activate the TSH receptor, driving excess thyroid hormone production and gland growth. They are central to Graves disease and guide diagnosis and management, especially where sophisticated tests are scarce.

b: Exophthalmos in up to 30 % of patients
sections.p: In Graves disease the immune system makes IgG antibodies that act like TSH, continuously turning the thyroid on. This explains the classic triad of diffuse goitre, hyperthyroidism and ophthalmopathy.

b: cAMP drives iodine organification and thyroglobulin synthesis
Chronic stimulation leads to gland enlargement (TGI component)
sections.p: TSI bind the extracellular domain of the TSH receptor (TSHR) on thyroid follicular cells, mimicking TSH. The receptor activates Gs protein → adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP → ↑ thyroid hormone synthesis and release, and also stimulates cell proliferation.

b: Low TSH despite high free T4/T3
sections.p: Normally TSH secretion from the pituitary is controlled by negative feedback from circulating T4/T3. TSI bypass this loop, so hormone levels rise despite low or suppressed TSH.
When TSI are present, the thyroid is over‑stimulated. The severity depends on antibody titre, duration, and co‑existing factors such as infection or iodine excess.

b: High relapse after antithyroid drugs if TSI remains positive
TSI positivity predicts response to radioiodine
Ophthalmopathy may need steroids or surgery
sections.p: Recognising TSI‑driven disease guides therapy (antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, surgery) and predicts relapse risk. In low‑resource settings, clinical clues often replace unavailable assays.

t.b: Is an autoimmune cause present? Positive result confirms Graves disease
What is the thyroid functional state? Elevated T4/T3 with suppressed TSH indicates thyrotoxicosis
Is the gland diffusely enlarged? Helps differentiate from toxic nodular goitre

b: TSI = functional auto‑antibody, not just a lab value
Low TSH + high T4/T3 + diffuse goitre → think Graves
In crisis (thyroid storm) treat urgently regardless of TSI result
sections.p: Focus on the pathophysiology linking antibody action to clinical signs, the diagnostic algorithm when TSI testing is unavailable, and management priorities in emergencies.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of tachycardia, fever, confusion or vomiting (possible thyroid storm)
Severe eye pain, vision loss or corneal ulceration
